summary: Workspace Example holds one product, Lists. Its Product Map links two specs. Lists (38,856 characters) has 8 sections and 15 element subsections (Inbox, Search, Sharing and All elements); Reminders (11,558 characters) has 7 sections and no subsection, its Direction one flat section of 3,919 characters that covers email and in-app reminders, quiet hours, days off, the digest, snoozed items and shared lists. Every pages read is served by the server's real outline and section reader over this content.

pages.title: Lists
pages.content:
# Lists

## Need

- When I plan my week, I want every item that needs me in one place, so nothing slips.
- When I start my day, I want to see first what is due today and what came back from snooze, so I begin with what matters instead of sorting.
- When an item cannot be done yet, I want to put it out of sight until a date, so my Inbox shows only what I can act on now.
- When I come back from a few days away, I want to see what piled up and what changed without me, so I can catch up in minutes rather than an afternoon.
- When I look for something I wrote weeks ago, I want to find it from a word, a list or a person, so I do not scroll through every list.
- When a project ends, I want its finished items out of my way without losing them, so I can still find what we decided.
- When I share a list with a client, I want them to see only what concerns them, so my private planning stays mine.
- When a guest comments on a shared item, I want every member of the list to see it, so nobody answers the same question twice.
- When I stop working with a client, I want to remove their access in one step, so nothing I add later reaches them.
- When I work across several lists, I want the same item to behave the same way wherever I meet it, so I never wonder which copy is true.
- When I am a guest on someone else's list, I want to know exactly what the owner can see of my account, so I can accept an invitation without worry.

## Outcome

People act on what needs them without hunting for it, find past work in seconds, and share a list without exposing the rest of their account. Signal: most items are completed from the Inbox rather than from inside a list; a search that a person follows by opening a result is the norm, not the exception; no guest reports seeing an item that was not shared with them; and owners who remove a guest do not report that the guest still received updates afterwards.

## Direction

### All elements

Lists move from one flat page to three elements a person moves between: the Inbox, Search and Sharing ([Lists roadmap](https://example.invalid/stream/lists-roadmap)). Each element works on the same items: an item lives in one list, and every element shows that one item, never a copy. A change made in one element appears in the others the next time they are shown.

The three elements share one way of showing an item (its title, its list, its date and the people on it) so a person who learns to read an item in one place can read it everywhere. An item's list is always named next to it, because the same title can mean different things in two projects. An item that is overdue shows how many days late it is rather than a colour alone, so the state reads without colour vision.

Keyboard use reaches every element: a person can move between the Inbox, Search and Sharing without a pointer, and every action an element offers has a key. Screen readers announce an item's title, list, date and state in that order in every element, so a person who listens learns one pattern.

The elements follow the person's language and time zone, never the list owner's, so a shared list reads correctly for each member. Dates show in the person's own format and week start.

Each element works on a slow connection: it shows what it already holds at once and marks what is still loading, instead of a blank screen, and an action taken while offline is kept and sent when the connection returns, with a mark on the item until it is sent. Two members who change the same item while one of them is offline both see the later change win, and the earlier one stays in the item's history so nothing typed is lost.

Every item keeps a history of its changes: who changed what and when, its comments, and its moves between lists and dates. A person opens the history from the item in any element and sees the same history. The history is kept as long as the item, and a restored item comes back with it, so the record of a decision survives a mistaken delete.

Lists can be brought in from a file of rows or from another tool's export, and taken out the same way. An import never merges into existing items: it creates new ones in the list the person chooses, and says how many rows it skipped and why, so a person can fix the file and bring in only what was missed. An export holds every field a person can see, in their language, so it can be read without the product.

Items carry the same small set of fields everywhere: title, notes, list, date, optional time, people, labels and state. A field that one element needs and the others do not belongs to that element's view of the item, never to the item, so the item stays the same object everywhere.

Labels belong to a person, not to a list, unless the list's owner makes a label part of the list; a shared label is visible to every member, a personal one only to the person who set it. Removing a label never removes the item.

Recurring items repeat on a rule the person sets (every day, every working day, every week on chosen days, every month on a date) and each occurrence is its own item, created when the previous one is done or when its date arrives, whichever comes first. Changing the rule changes the occurrences still to come and never the ones already done.

Every element answers within the time a person notices as instant for the actions they repeat most (opening the Inbox, typing in Search, marking an item done) on an ordinary phone and connection, and shows progress for anything slower. When an element cannot meet that, it shows what it has and keeps loading, never freezing the screen.

The product explains itself in place: the first time a person meets an element, one short line says what it is for and how to leave it, and the line does not come back once dismissed. Help never covers an item the person is trying to act on.

Each element can be reached from a link that names it, so a person can send a colleague straight to a shared list's item, and the link opens only for someone who can see that item; for anyone else it says the item is not available, without saying whether it exists.

Large accounts keep working: a person with thousands of items and hundreds of lists sees the same speed in the Inbox and Search as a new account, because those elements read only what they show. A list with many items opens on its first screen at once and loads the rest as the person scrolls.

Archiving a list takes it out of the Inbox and out of ordinary Search results while keeping every item, comment and member; an archived shared list stays visible to its members as archived, and only its owner restores it. Archiving is the way to end a project without deleting anything, and the product offers it before delete whenever a person tries to delete a list with items.

Deleting a list moves it and its items to the trash for 30 days, with notice to its members if it is shared; restoring it brings back its items, comments and members as they were, and members regain access without a new invitation.

Notifications from every element go through one place in the person's settings, where they choose, for each reason (assigned, due, mentioned, comment on an item they follow, back from snooze), whether it reaches them in the app, by email or not at all; an element never sends a notification the person turned off there.

### Inbox

The Inbox becomes the default place to start the day. It groups items by the date they need the person, then by list. Items snoozed to a later date leave the Inbox until that date and come back at the top of their day. A later step lets a person snooze a whole list at once, so a paused project stops crowding the day ([Inbox snooze](https://example.invalid/task/inbox-snooze)).

An item enters the Inbox when it needs the person: it is assigned to them, it is due within the coming week, someone mentions them on it, or a snooze they set ends. An item leaves the Inbox when it is done, when it is reassigned to someone else, when its date moves beyond the coming week, or when the person snoozes it. Items without a date that need the person sit in a group of their own below the dated groups, so they are visible without pushing dated work down.

The person can mark an item done, snooze it, move it to another date or open it from the Inbox itself, without opening its list. Marking an item done removes it from the Inbox at once and keeps an undo for a short time, so a mistaken tap costs nothing. Snoozing offers the next morning, the next working day, the next week and a chosen date; a person who snoozes often sees the choice they use most first.

The Inbox shows how many items each day holds, so a person sees an overloaded day before it arrives. A later step suggests moving items from an overloaded day to a lighter one, and applies the move only on the person's yes ([Day balancing](https://example.invalid/task/day-balancing)).

After a person has been away for more than two days, the Inbox opens on a short catch-up: the items that became due while they were away, the items others changed or commented on, and the items assigned to them meanwhile, each group with its count. The catch-up closes once the person has seen it and does not come back for the same absence. Items in it are the same items as in the dated groups, so acting on one in the catch-up acts on it everywhere.

Mentions bring an item into the Inbox for three days, or until the person opens it, whichever comes first, so a mention is noticed without staying forever. A mention on an item already in the Inbox marks it rather than adding it twice.

Overdue items stay at the top of today, ordered by how late they are, until they are done, moved or snoozed. The Inbox never hides an overdue item on its own, because a forgotten deadline is the failure the Inbox exists to prevent.

A person can pin up to a handful of items to the top of the Inbox for the day; pins clear the next morning, so the Inbox does not fill with old pins. Pinned items keep their date and come back to their own day once the pin clears.

On a small screen the Inbox shows today first and folds the other days, so the first screen is always what needs the person now. Swiping an item offers done and snooze, the two actions people take most.

A weekly review, offered on the day the person chooses, walks through the items with no date, the items overdue for more than a week, and the lists with nothing done in a month, one group at a time, and lets the person date, snooze, delegate or archive each item in place. The review ends when the person has seen every group or closes it, and it never runs on its own.

Delegating an item from the Inbox assigns it to another member of its list and takes it out of the person's Inbox; the person who delegated can follow it, which keeps it visible in a followed group without counting it as theirs to do. A followed item leaves that group when it is done.

A focus view shows only today and the items the person pinned, hides counts and other days, and keeps every action available. It ends at the end of the day or when the person leaves it, so nobody stays in focus by accident.

Recurring items show only their next occurrence in the Inbox, never a run of future ones, so a daily item does not fill the week.

When the person changes time zone, the Inbox regroups items by the days of the new zone at once, and a snooze set for a date ends at the start of that date where the person is, not where they were.

The Inbox counts are shown only for days, never as a total of everything open, because a large total discourages more than it informs.

An item the person cannot open any more, because it was moved to a list they lost access to or deleted by its owner, leaves their Inbox at once and leaves no trace there, while their own past actions on it stay in the item's history for the list's members.

Items in the Inbox carry a short reason for being there, in plain words (assigned to you, due Thursday, mentioned by a member, back from snooze), so a person understands at a glance why an item needs them and can act on the reason, for example by snoozing a mention without changing the item's date.

A person can turn off the reasons they do not want in the Inbox, for example mentions on lists they only follow, and the Inbox says in its settings which reasons are off, so an empty Inbox is never a surprise. Assigned and due items cannot be turned off, because they are what the Inbox is for.

When a list is snoozed as a whole, once that step comes, its items leave the Inbox together and come back together on the chosen date, each at the top of its own day, and an item of that list that someone else assigns to the person during the snooze still comes in, marked as belonging to a snoozed list.

Items done in the Inbox today stay visible in a folded group at the end of today until the next morning, so a person can see what they finished and undo a mistaken completion after the short undo has passed.

The Inbox never reorders items while the person looks at it; new items arrive with a mark at the place they belong, and the order settles the next time the Inbox opens, so a person never taps an item that moved under their finger.

A person who has nothing in the Inbox for today sees that plainly, with tomorrow's count, and no prompt to add work.

The Inbox can be filtered to one list or one label for a moment, for a person who wants to clear one project; the filter shows plainly at the top and clears when the Inbox is closed, so nobody forgets that part of their work is hidden.

When a person is assigned many items at once, for example when a colleague hands over a project, the Inbox gathers them into one group named for the handover, with a count, instead of spreading them over the days; the person can open the group and date the items, or accept their dates as they are, in one step.

The Inbox reads the same on every device a person uses: an item done on the phone is gone from the computer's Inbox the next time it is shown, and a snooze set on one device holds on all of them.

A person who works part of the week can mark their working days, and the Inbox then counts and groups only those days: an item due on a day off shows on the last working day before it, marked with its real date, so nothing due over a weekend arrives as a surprise on Monday. Snoozing to the next working day uses the same days.

An item the person adds from the Inbox goes to their default list, which they choose once, and takes today's date unless they give another, so a quick capture during the day lands where they will see it again. The Inbox never asks which list before saving, because asking costs the thought the person wanted to capture.

When the Inbox holds more items for today than a person can see on one screen, it shows the count of what is below and keeps overdue and pinned items on the first screen, so the items most at risk are never the ones scrolled out of sight.

### Search

Search finds items by their words, their list and their people. Archived items stay out of results unless the person asks for them, so finished work does not crowd current work. A later step adds saved searches that a person can pin beside the Inbox ([Saved searches](https://example.invalid/task/saved-searches)).

Results come back as the person types, ordered by how well they match and then by how recently the item changed. Each result shows where the match was found, the title, the text or a comment, so a person can tell at a glance whether it is the item they want. Filters narrow results by list, by person, by date range and by state (open, done or archived); the filters a person sets stay in place while they refine their words.

Search understands simple forms of words, so "invoice" finds "invoices" and "invoiced". It does not guess at meaning beyond that: a person who searches for a word sees items that contain it, not items an algorithm thinks are related, because people need to trust that a missing result means the word is not there. Quoted words match exactly, and a minus sign before a word leaves out items that contain it.

A person can search inside one list from that list, and across all their lists from anywhere. Search across lists covers every list the person can open, their own and the ones shared with them, and nothing else. When a person loses access to a list, its items leave their results at once, not at the next refresh.

Opening a result takes the person to the item in its list, with the matching words highlighted, and a way back to the results with the search still in place.

Recent searches are kept for each person, never shared, and a person can clear them. A search with no result says so plainly and offers to include archived items when they were left out, because that is the most common reason a person does not find what they wrote.

Search works on items written in any of the languages the product offers, and matches word forms in the language the item is written in, so a list kept in two languages is searchable in both.

Saved searches, once they come, keep their words and filters and show a count of matching open items; pinning one beside the Inbox shows that count there, so a person can follow a theme without searching again. A saved search sees only what its owner can see at the moment it runs, never what they could see when they saved it.

Search results load in pages as the person scrolls, and the count of results is shown as an estimate when it is large, because an exact count on a large account would slow every search.

Search inside a list offers the list's own labels and members as filters first, because they are what a person narrows by within a project.

From a result, a person can act on the item without opening it: mark it done, change its date or snooze it, with the same undo as everywhere else. Acting on a result keeps it in the results, marked with its new state, so the list of results does not jump under the person's hand.

A search can be turned into a list of items to work through: the person selects results and moves them together to a date, a person or a list, and sees before confirming how many items will change and in which lists. Moving items between lists by this route follows the same rule as moving one item, so an item moved into a shared list becomes visible to its members.

Deleted items do not appear in results; items in the trash are searchable from the trash only, so a person who looks for something they deleted can find it without it crowding ordinary results.

On a small screen, Search opens with the person's recent searches and their saved searches, and the filters fold into one row that opens on a tap.

Search keeps its results correct as items change: an item edited while its result is on screen shows its new text the next time the results refresh, and an item the person can no longer open disappears from the results on that refresh, never staying clickable.

Search never ranks one member's items above another's, and never learns from what a person opens, because people must get the same results for the same words.

Typing in Search never sends the words anywhere but the person's own account's search, and searches are not used for anything else.

Search speaks in plain terms when something goes wrong: a search that cannot run says so and keeps the words in place to try again, and never shows an empty result in place of an error.

Search offers a short list of suggestions as the person types: lists and members whose names match, then items, so a person who types a list's name can jump to the list instead of searching its contents. Suggestions never include anything the person cannot open.

Search inside comments shows the comment with its author and date in the result, and opening it takes the person to that comment in the item, not only to the item.

When a list is archived, its items count as archived in Search, so the archived filter brings back a whole finished project at once. Restoring the list brings its items back into ordinary results.

Search treats the item's title as the strongest match and its notes and comments after, so an item named for the word comes first; within the same strength, the most recently changed item comes first.

Search respects each list's language setting for word forms, and an item without a set language is matched by the language of its text when that can be told with confidence, and by exact words otherwise.

When results include items from shared lists, each result names its list and the list's owner, so a person can tell their own work from a client's.

A person can search by date words such as today, this week or overdue, and by state words such as done, alongside ordinary words, and Search shows the filter it understood so the person can correct it.

Search keeps the person's place: leaving Search and coming back within the same session shows the same words, filters and scroll position, so checking a result and returning costs nothing.

An owner's search across lists shows items written by guests in the owner's shared lists, like any other item of those lists, and a guest's search shows only the lists shared with them, never the owner's other lists.

Search can be reached from every screen with one key or one tap, and opens with the person's place in the product as a starting filter (the list they are in, or the Inbox), which they can clear to search everything.

A person who searches for a member's name sees that member's items and the items that mention them, in two groups, because what someone owns and what someone was asked about are different questions.

### Sharing

A person shares a list with a guest by email. The guest sees the shared list and nothing else of the owner's account. Comments on a shared item reach every member of the list. A later step adds view-only guests for clients who must not edit ([View-only guests](https://example.invalid/task/view-only-guests)).

An invitation names the list and the person who sends it, and it expires after two weeks if nobody accepts it. A guest who accepts joins that one list as a member who can add items, edit them, mark them done and comment. A guest who has no account creates one from the invitation; that account holds no lists of its own until the guest makes one.

Before accepting, the guest sees what joining means: the name of the list, who else is on it, and that the owner and other members will see their name, their email and what they write in that list, and nothing else of their account.

The owner sees every member of a list and how each one joined, and removes a member in one step. A removed member loses access at once: the list disappears from their account, their pending notifications for it are withdrawn, and nothing added afterwards reaches them. The items and comments they wrote stay in the list, marked with their name, because the work belongs to the list.

When a list is shared, its items show the members assigned to them, and assigning an item to a guest puts it in that guest's Inbox like any other item. Mentions work across members of the list only; a person cannot mention someone who is not a member, so a mention never leaks an item to an outsider.

An owner can stop sharing a list entirely, which removes every guest at once, and can share it again later with new invitations.

Moving an item from a shared list to a private one removes it from every guest's view at once, and moving an item into a shared list shows it to every member; the person who moves it sees, before confirming, who will gain or lose sight of it.

A guest can leave a list on their own at any time; the owner is told, and the guest's items and comments stay, as for a removed member.

Ownership of a list can pass to another member who already has an account, on both people's yes; the former owner becomes a member and keeps their access unless the new owner removes them. A list always has exactly one owner.

Comments on a shared item show who wrote them and when, can be edited by their author for a short time, and can be deleted by their author or by the owner; a deleted comment leaves a mark saying it was deleted, so a thread stays readable.

Guests receive notifications only for the shared list, by the channels they chose in their own account; an owner cannot change a guest's notification settings.

An activity view on each shared list shows who joined, who left, who was removed and when invitations were sent, accepted or expired, so the owner can answer the question of who had access and when. Members see the same view, because people on a list should know who else is on it.

A guest who replies to a notification email adds a comment to the item, under their name, and the reply is refused with an explanation if they have since been removed.

An owner can set, per shared list, whether members may move items out of the list; when they may not, only the owner moves items out, because moving an item out of a shared list removes it from every member's view.

When the owner's account closes, every list they own is offered to its members, one owner per list, on that member's yes; a list nobody takes is kept in the trash for 30 days and then removed, with notice to every member at the start of that time.

Invitations can be sent again, which extends the two weeks from the new sending, and withdrawn before they are accepted, after which the link in the email no longer opens anything.

A member's view of the list is the same as the owner's for items, comments and members, except the owner's settings for the list, which only the owner sees and changes.

View-only guests, once they come, see items and comments and can comment but not add, edit, move or complete items; the owner can change a member between full and view-only at any time, effective at once.

Sharing settings are part of the list, not of the account: a person who owns several lists sets each one, and copying a list copies its items but none of its members.

A person can see, from their own account, every list shared with them and every list they share, with the members of each, so they can review their sharing in one place and leave or remove access from there.

Shared lists are marked as shared wherever they appear, in the Inbox, in Search results and in the list itself, so a person always knows when what they write will be seen by others.

The owner can export the list's activity view, so a client relationship's access history can be kept outside the product when a contract requires it.

When a guest is also a member of several of the owner's lists, each list keeps its own membership; removing the guest from one list never touches the others, and the owner sees, when removing, which other lists the guest is still on.

A guest's items in a shared list follow the list's rules, not the guest's own account settings, so an owner's choice of who may move items out holds for every member.

Members can leave a note on their membership visible to the owner, such as their role on the project, so a long list of members stays understandable.

Before an owner shares a list that holds items assigned to people outside it, the owner is told which items those are and that their assignees will not see them unless they join, so sharing never changes who works on an item without the owner knowing.

An owner who shares many lists with the same client can send one invitation for several lists; the guest accepts or declines each list separately, because consent is per list.

When a member's email address changes, their membership follows their account, not their old address, and pending invitations to the old address stay pending until withdrawn or expired.

A guest who is removed while an item of the list sits in their Inbox loses that item from their Inbox at once, with no trace, and an item they had snoozed simply never returns.

Owners can preview the list as a guest sees it, from the list's sharing settings, to check what a new guest will find before sending an invitation; the preview shows the list's items, comments and members and nothing of the owner's other lists.

When an invitation reaches someone who already has an account under another address, they can accept it into that account after confirming the invited address belongs to them, so a person never ends up with two accounts to follow one client.

## Choices

### All elements

- One item belongs to exactly one list, because moving an item between lists must never duplicate it (Decision "One list per item").
- Every element reads the same item record and none keeps its own copy, because a copy drifts and people stop trusting what they see.
- Dates are stored as days, not as times, unless a person sets a time, because most items are due on a day and a time zone shift must never move a due date to the day before.
- Keyboard actions use the same keys in every element, because people learn them once.
- When two changes to an item conflict, the later one wins and the earlier one stays in the item's history, because merging text silently produces sentences nobody wrote.
- An action taken offline is kept and sent later rather than refused, because people plan on trains and planes.
- Recurring items create one occurrence at a time, because a calendar full of future copies cannot be changed in one place.
- Import never merges into existing items, because a wrong merge loses text a person cannot see was lost.
- Labels are personal unless a list's owner shares them, because one person's way of sorting should not reshape a shared list.
- Links to items reveal nothing to people who cannot see the item, because even an item's existence can be private.

### Inbox

- The Inbox orders by date before list, because people plan by day, not by project.
- Snoozing is personal to the person who snoozes, because two members of a list may plan the same item differently; see Promises, Sharing, for what a guest sees of a snoozed item.
- An item that returns from snooze goes to the top of its day, not to its old place, because a person who snoozed it chose to meet it again first.
- Undated items that need the person sit below the dated groups rather than in a separate tab, because a separate tab is forgotten.
- Day balancing only suggests and never moves an item on its own, because a person's plan is theirs to change.
- The catch-up appears only after more than two days away, because a shorter absence is covered by the dated groups and a catch-up every morning would be noise.
- Overdue items stay at the top of today until a person acts on them, because hiding them would let deadlines pass unseen.
- Pins clear each morning, because a pin that lasts becomes a second list nobody tends.
- Recurring items show one occurrence at a time, because a run of future occurrences buries today's work.
- The focus view ends with the day, because a mode that persists is forgotten and hides work.
- Counts are per day, never a grand total, because a large total discourages without telling a person what to do next.
- Reasons for an item's presence are shown in words, because a person must know why an item needs them to decide what to do with it.
- Assigned and due items cannot be turned off, because an Inbox that can hide them stops being the place nothing slips through.
- The Inbox never reorders while open, because an item that moves under a finger is acted on by mistake.

### Search

- Search reads the item's text and comments, never its attachments, because attachments may hold data the owner never meant to index.
- Archived items are excluded by default and included by one filter, because finished work is rarely what a person looks for but must stay findable.
- Matching uses word forms and nothing broader, because people must be able to trust that an empty result means the word is absent.
- Results order by match first and recency second, because the best match is what a person usually wants and recency breaks ties in a way people expect.
- Recent searches stay private to each person, because what someone looked for can reveal what they are worried about.
- A saved search runs with the access its owner has when it runs, because access changes and a saved search must never outlive it.
- Large result counts are estimates, because an exact count would slow every search on a large account.
- Acting on a result keeps it in the list of results, because results that move while a person works make them lose their place.
- Search does not learn from what a person opens, because the same words must give the same results.
- An error is shown as an error, never as an empty result, because an empty result says the word is absent.
- Titles weigh more than notes and comments, because people name items for what they are.
- Date and state words are understood and shown back as filters, because people type them anyway and need to see how they were read.

### Sharing

- A guest is invited per list, never per account, because owners share one project at a time.
- Invitations expire after two weeks, because a forgotten invitation should not open a list months later.
- Items and comments of a removed member stay in the list, because the work belongs to the list and its history must stay whole.
- Mentions are limited to members of the list, because a mention that reaches an outsider would reveal the item.
- A guest sees, before accepting, what the list's members will see of them, because consent needs to know what it consents to.
- Ownership passes only on both people's yes, because a list must never land on someone who did not agree to own it.
- A deleted comment leaves a mark, because a thread with silent gaps misleads its readers.
- Guests set their own notifications, because an owner deciding how a guest is contacted would reach into the guest's account.
- Members see the list's activity view too, because people should know who else is on a list they work in.
- Copying a list copies no members, because access must always be granted on purpose.
- One invitation may cover several lists but each is accepted separately, because consent is per list.
- Membership follows the account, not the address, because people change addresses and must not lose access by doing so.

## Promises

### All elements

- A person's item is never lost: deleting moves it to a trash kept 30 days, and an item in the trash can be restored to its list with its comments.
- An item shows the same title, list, date and people in every element at the same moment.
- Every action that changes an item can be undone for a short time after it is made.
- Text typed while offline is never lost: it is sent when the connection returns or kept in the item's history if a later change wins.
- No element shows an item's state by colour alone.
- A link to an item never reveals whether the item exists to someone who cannot see it.
- Archiving or deleting a shared list always tells its members.

### Inbox

- The Inbox never shows an item the person cannot open.
- An item snoozed until a date never appears in the Inbox before that date, and always appears on it unless it was done or deleted meanwhile.
- Marking an item done from the Inbox never changes anything else about the item.
- The Inbox never hides an overdue item on its own.
- A change of time zone never makes a snoozed item return before its date where the person is.
- An item added from the Inbox is never saved to a list other than the person's chosen default unless they pick one.

### Search

- Search never returns an item from a list the person cannot see.
- Search never shows text from an attachment.
- A result that a person can open always opens the item it names.
- A person's recent and saved searches are never shown to anyone else.
- Suggestions never name a list, member or item the person cannot open.

### Sharing

- A guest never sees an item of a list not shared with them.
- A guest never sees who snoozed an item or until when.
- A removed member receives nothing about the list after their removal, not even a notification queued before it.
- An owner can always see every member of their list and how each one joined.
- Nobody joins a list without accepting an invitation to it.
- A guest's account shows nothing of theirs to a list's members beyond their name, their email and what they write in that list.
- An invitation that was withdrawn or expired never opens the list.
- A guest's notification settings are never changed by anyone but the guest.
- Removing a guest from one list never changes their access to any other list.

## Non-goals

### Sharing

- Public links open to anyone: lists hold private work; publishing belongs to Pages ([Pages spec](https://example.invalid/page/pages-spec)).
- Sharing a single item outside its list: an item takes its meaning from its list, and a lone item would need its own membership; people who need this share the list or copy the text.
- Account-wide guests: owners share one project at a time, and an account-wide guest would see work never meant for them.
- Guests who can invite other guests: the owner must always know who is in a list.
- Roles beyond owner, member and the coming view-only guest: each new role multiplies what a person must understand before sharing, and no request so far needs one.
- Sharing with a whole organization by its email domain: membership must be a decision about each person, not a rule that adds people silently.

## Open questions

### Inbox

- [open] Whether a snoozed item that comes back should notify the person.
- [open] Whether undated items that need the person should age into the current day after a week, so they are not forgotten.
- [open] Whether the catch-up should count days away from the last time the person opened the Inbox or from the last time they acted on an item.
- [idea 2026-10-21] Let a person set the hour their Inbox day starts, for people who work at night; read the Night shift notes before assessing or building it.
- [open] Whether a person on leave should be able to pause their Inbox so that assignments go back to the assigner.

### Search

- [idea 2026-11-02] Search across every list a team shares; read [Team search notes](https://example.invalid/page/team-search-notes) before assessing or building it.
- [open] Whether saved searches should be shareable with the members of a list.
- [open] Whether attachments' file names, unlike their contents, may be searched.
- [open] Whether items written by a removed member should still show their name in results, or the list's name only.

## Links

[Product Map](https://example.invalid/page/product-map) · [Architecture Map](https://example.invalid/page/architecture-map) · Decision "One list per item" · [Pages spec](https://example.invalid/page/pages-spec) · [Reminders spec](https://example.invalid/page/reminders-spec)

pages.title: Reminders
pages.content:
# Reminders

## Need

- When an item has a date, I want to be reminded before it, so I am never surprised by a deadline.
- When I am busy in another tool, I want a reminder to reach me where I already look, so I do not have to keep the product open all day.
- When I sleep or rest, I want reminders to wait for my morning, so a deadline does not wake me.
- When many items fall on the same day, I want one summary rather than a stream of messages, so reminders help me plan instead of interrupting me.
- When I put an item off on purpose, I want it to stay quiet until I chose to meet it again, so a reminder does not undo my decision.
- When I work on a list shared with others, I want reminders only for what is mine, so I am not reminded of a colleague's work.
- When a reminder reaches me, I want to act on the item from the reminder itself, so a reminder costs one tap, not a search.
- When I am away for a holiday, I want reminders to stop and to tell me on my return what I missed, so I come back to a plan rather than a pile of messages.
- When an item matters more than most, I want more warning for it, so the important deadlines never arrive on the day itself.
- When I hand an item to a colleague, I want the reminders to follow the item to them, so I stop being reminded of work that is no longer mine.
- When I change an item's date, I want its reminders to move with it, so I am never reminded of a date that no longer holds.

## Outcome

People hear about a dated item early enough to act, without reminders becoming noise they learn to ignore. Signal: few items are completed after their date; people who receive reminders keep them turned on after their first month; few reminders are dismissed without the item being opened, done or moved; and people who use the digest open it on most days it arrives.

## Direction

Reminders reach the person by email and in the app the morning an item is due, and a day before when the item is marked important. An in-app reminder appears in the app's notification area and on the person's phone when they installed the app, and it disappears from every device once the person opens it on one. An email reminder names the item, its list and its date, and offers to open the item, to mark it done and to move it to tomorrow, each with one tap, without signing in again when the person is already signed in on that device. A person chooses, in their settings, whether reminders reach them by email, in the app, or both, and both is the starting choice for a new account. Quiet hours hold every reminder until the person's morning. A person sets their quiet hours once, and the starting quiet hours run from nine in the evening to eight in the morning in the person's own time zone. A reminder that falls inside quiet hours is sent when they end, in the order the items are due, and a reminder held overnight is never sent twice. When the person travels, quiet hours follow the time zone of the device they use, so the morning is their morning where they are. A person can also set days off, such as a holiday, during which no reminder is sent at all. On the first morning after days off, one message lists the items that became due during the absence and the items due that day, so the person catches up in one read. A digest gathers a day's reminders into one email for people who choose it ([Reminder digest](https://example.invalid/task/reminder-digest)). The digest arrives when quiet hours end and lists the items due that day, then the items due the next day that are marked important, each with the same one-tap actions as a single reminder. A person who chooses the digest receives no separate email reminders for the items it lists, while in-app reminders keep coming one by one. A day with nothing due sends no digest. The digest groups items by list when it holds more than a handful, so a person can see at a glance which project the day belongs to. A snoozed item sends no reminder until its snooze ends. When the snooze ends, the item is treated as due that day for reminders, so the person hears about it once in the morning of its return, and an item snoozed past its own date is reminded on the day it returns, marked as overdue. A whole list snoozed at once, once that step comes in Lists, silences the reminders of all its items in the same way and brings them back together. Shared lists remind each member who owns the item, never the guests. An item of a shared list with no assignee reminds the list's owner only, so a guest is never reminded of work that was not given to them. An item assigned to a guest reminds that guest like any other item assigned to them, by the channels the guest chose in their own account. A member removed from a shared list stops receiving its reminders at once, including any held by their quiet hours. A recurring item reminds only for its next occurrence, never for occurrences still to come. An item whose date changes after its reminder was scheduled is reminded for its new date only, and an item done before its reminder is sent sends none. An email reminder is written in the person's own language, and its dates follow their own format. A person can snooze an item from the reminder itself, with the same choices as in the Inbox, and the snooze silences that item's reminders like any other. When a reminder cannot be delivered by email, for example because the address bounces, the in-app reminder still arrives and the person's settings show that email reminders are failing, so a broken address does not silently swallow every deadline. A person who opens the app before their morning reminder sees the same items in the Inbox, and the reminder is then still sent, because the Inbox and reminders serve different moments.

## Choices

- Reminders follow the person's time zone, never the list owner's, because members of one list live in different places.
- Email and in-app reminders say the same thing, because a person reads whichever comes first.
- The important flag adds a reminder the day before rather than changing the morning reminder, because people who flag an item want more warning, not a different message.
- Quiet hours hold reminders rather than dropping them, because a reminder that never arrives is worse than a late one.
- Quiet hours follow the device's time zone, because a person who travels wants their own morning, not their home's.
- Days off stop reminders entirely and end with one catch-up message, because a stream of held reminders on the first morning back would bury the day.
- The digest replaces single email reminders for the items it lists, because two emails about one item teach people to ignore both.
- The digest is sent only on days with something due, because an empty digest trains people to delete it unread.
- The digest is an email only, because the in-app reminders already arrive one by one where the person works.
- Reminders go to the item's assignee, or to the owner when nobody is assigned, because a reminder sent to everyone on a list is a reminder nobody acts on.
- A snooze silences reminders until it ends, because a person who snoozes an item has chosen when to meet it again.
- An item back from snooze is reminded once, on the morning of its return, because the return itself is the moment the person chose.
- Actions in a reminder work without signing in again on a device where the person is signed in, because a reminder that leads to a sign-in page is abandoned.
- Reminders carry no tracking of whether an email was opened, because reading habits are the person's own business.
- Recurring items remind for one occurrence at a time, because a reminder for each future occurrence would fill the week with copies.
- A reminder follows the item's current date and assignee at the moment it is sent, not when it was scheduled, because dates and owners change and a stale reminder misleads.
- Email failures surface in the person's settings rather than in a separate warning email, because a warning sent to a failing address never arrives.
- Reminder emails are written in the recipient's language, not the list owner's, because each member reads their own.
- Snoozing from a reminder offers the same choices as the Inbox, because one way to snooze is easier to learn than two.
- Days off are set by the person, never inferred from their activity, because a quiet week is not always a holiday.
- The catch-up after days off is one message, not a digest per missed day, because a person returning wants one picture of what changed.
- Reminders stay on by default for a new account, because a person who never hears about a deadline learns nothing from the product.
- The day-before reminder for an important item arrives when quiet hours end, like the morning one, because more warning is no reason to break a person's rest.

## Promises

- A person can turn every reminder off in one place.
- A reminder never reveals an item's text in an email subject when the list is marked private.
- A reminder held by quiet hours is never lost and never sent twice.
- A guest is never reminded of an item that is not assigned to them.
- A snoozed item never sends a reminder before its snooze ends.
- An action taken from a reminder changes only what it names.
- A reminder never reaches someone who has lost access to the item's list, even if it was queued before.
- Turning reminders off takes effect at once, including for reminders already held by quiet hours.
- No reminder is sent during a person's days off.
- A reminder always names the item's list, so a person can tell two items of the same title apart.
- A reminder never contains a link that opens the item for someone other than its recipient.
- An item reassigned to someone else stops reminding its former assignee at once.
- An item done or deleted sends no reminder afterwards, even one already scheduled.
- A person whose email reminders fail can always see that they fail in their settings.
- A reminder never shows the names of members who snoozed the item or when.

## Non-goals

- Text messages: their cost and consent rules outweigh their value for now.
- Reminders at a chosen minute for every item: most items are due on a day, and minute-level reminders belong to a calendar, which people already use for meetings.
- Reminding people who are not members of a list, such as a client's colleague by email address alone: reminders follow membership, and anyone who needs them can be invited.
- Escalating a missed item to a manager: Lists has no notion of a manager, and an escalation would turn a planning tool into a monitoring one.
- Read receipts on reminders: they would tell others when a person read their messages.
- Reminders through chat tools: each tool needs its own consent and settings, and email and the app already reach people where they look.
- Reminders that repeat until acted on: a reminder that nags is soon turned off, and the Inbox already keeps an overdue item in view.
- Reminders for items without a date: an undated item has no moment to remind about; the Inbox keeps undated items that need a person in view.
- Location-based reminders: they need a person's location, which Lists does not collect and has no reason to.
- Reminding a whole team of a shared deadline at once: reminders follow the item's assignee or owner; a shared deadline is an item assigned to each person who must act on it.
